comparison: Both address lysosomal Ca2+ measurements using GCaMP3-ML1 (C22, C23). OpenEval finds the data well-supported by multiple complementary measurements. Peer reviewers fundamentally reject this result as 'highly problematic' due to transient transfection issues in BMDMs, stating 'efficiency of transfection in BMDMs is always extremely low' and 'overexpression results in gross mislocalization' preventing credible measurements.

OpenEval R1 addresses cytosolic Ca2+ measurements (C1, C2) as part of comprehensive support for lysosomal Ca2+ depletion. Peer R2 challenges these cytosolic Ca2+ measurements (C1, C2), stating 'figure 1C doesn't make any sense' and that 'snapshot measurements are not helpful' for dynamic Ca2+ elevations.

Both evaluate BAPTA-AM effects on IL-1β release (C24-C27). OpenEval finds the data support that BAPTA-AM's effect is unrelated to transcription/translation inhibition. Peer reviewers challenge this interpretation, stating 'BAPTA-AM abrogates IL-1β secretion because IL-1β transcription is Ca2+ dependent' and that the result 'is misleading to suggest that' it relates to inflammasome activation.

Both address ROS production claims (C28-C36). OpenEval finds the data well-supported by CM-H2DCFDA and MitoSOX measurements showing synergistic ROS production and functional validation with antioxidants. Peer reviewers do not directly critique these ROS data, appearing to accept them as supporting mechanistic evidence.

Both evaluate TRPM2 localization and function (C37-C44). OpenEval finds the colocalization and pharmacological data supportive. Peer reviewers raise fundamental concerns: 'TRPM2 is a lysosomal ion channel' is 'a controversial claim, with no replication,' localization data show 'very high amounts of TRPM2 all across the cell,' and 'Apigenin and Quercetin are highly non-specific.'

Both address TRPM2 knockout effects on Ca2+ dynamics and inflammasome (C45-C52). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from multiple measurements. Peer reviewers question the underlying TRPM2 localization and function claims, with concerns about whether TRPM2 is truly lysosomal and whether the data quality supports the conclusions.

Both evaluate TRPM2 selectivity for different inflammasome activators (C53-C57). OpenEval finds the differential effects provide strong evidence for lysosomal TRPM2 specificity. Peer reviewers' concerns about TRPM2 localization and function (from R3) extend to questioning the interpretation of these selectivity data.

Both address in vivo metabolic phenotype of Trpm2 KO mice (C58-C67). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from glucose measurements, IPGTT, histology, and inflammasome markers. Peer reviewers challenge the mechanistic attribution, stating 'The broad metabolic differences observed...cannot be attributed to macrophage-mediated inflammation' without cell-type-specific deletion.

Both evaluate plasma membrane vs lysosomal TRPM2 using patch clamp (C68-C76). OpenEval finds the data provide strong evidence for lysosomal versus plasma membrane TRPM2. Peer reviewers reject this, stating the patch clamp data are 'of very poor quality,' questioning whether results represent 'leak currents,' noting 'Trpm2-/- controls are missing,' and that '20 uM ACA is not a selective inhibitor.'

Both address ER→lysosome Ca2+ flux (C77-C81). OpenEval finds strong support from GEM-CEPIA1er and D1ER measurements showing temporal correlation. Peer reviewers fundamentally reject this, stating 'ER-Lysosome Ca2+ refilling experiments rely on transient transfection' which is 'highly problematic,' and 'the data procured are also not convincing and lack critical controls.'

Both evaluate IP3R involvement in ER→lysosome Ca2+ transfer (C82-C88). OpenEval finds support from Xestospongin C and TPEN effects. Peer reviewers reject the underlying ER-lysosome Ca2+ refilling data due to transfection issues and lack of controls, undermining these mechanistic claims.

Both address VAPA-ORP1L contacts facilitating Ca2+ refilling (C89-C90). OpenEval finds PLA data supportive though mechanistic link not directly tested. Peer reviewers' rejection of the ER-lysosome Ca2+ refilling approach extends to questioning these contact site data.

Both evaluate SOCE activation and its role in inflammasome (C91-C98). OpenEval finds support from pharmacological inhibitors and D1ER measurements. Peer reviewers state 'there is no credible evidence that SOCE is activated,' criticizing 'snapshot measurements and crude non-selective inhibitors,' and stating 'the only definitive way' is patch clamp electrophysiology.

Both address STIM1-ORAI1 colocalization as evidence of SOCE (C99-C101). OpenEval finds confocal microscopy data supportive. Peer reviewers' rejection of SOCE activation evidence extends to questioning whether these colocalization data demonstrate functional SOCE in this context.

Both evaluate K+ efflux coupling to SOCE and ER Ca2+ (C102-C109). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from multiple measurements. Peer reviewers note that while K+ measurements themselves aren't questioned, the mechanistic interpretation linking them to SOCE is uncertain given the challenged SOCE activation evidence.

Both address KCa3.1 channel identification and selectivity (C110-C119). OpenEval finds systematic pharmacological profiling supportive. Peer reviewers do not directly critique these data, and the pharmacological specificity with TRAM-34 and Kcnn4 KO validation appear accepted.

Both evaluate KCa3.1's positive role in Ca2+ influx and K+ efflux (C120-C125). OpenEval finds support from TRAM-34 effects on multiple Ca2+ and K+ measurements. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these KCa3.1 functional data.

Both address SOCE inhibition preventing KCa3.1 activation (C126-C128). OpenEval finds the inference logical based on BTP2 effects. Peer reviewers' concerns about SOCE evidence may extend to this coupling claim, though the KCa3.1 data themselves are not directly challenged.

Both evaluate nystatin-perforated patch clamp data showing KCa3.1 activation (C129-C133). OpenEval finds strong support including Kcnn4 KO validation. Peer reviewers do not critique these electrophysiological measurements, in contrast to their concerns about TRPM2 patch clamp data.

Both address Kcnn4 KO effects on inflammasome and K+ efflux (C134-C139). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from genetic validation. Peer reviewers do not challenge these Kcnn4 KO data, and the genetic approach with specificity for inflammasome appears accepted.

Both evaluate TRAM-34 preventing lysosomal Ca2+ recovery (C140-C141). OpenEval finds support linking K+ efflux to ER→lysosome refilling. Peer reviewers' rejection of the ER-lysosome Ca2+ refilling measurements may extend to questioning this mechanistic link.

Both address KCNN4-ORAI1 contacts and their functional significance (C142-C145). OpenEval notes functional significance is speculative. Peer reviewers do not directly critique these PLA data, though the underlying SOCE concerns may affect interpretation.

Both evaluate Kcnn4 KO selectivity for different inflammasome activators (C146-C150). OpenEval finds the selectivity pattern provides strong evidence. Peer reviewers do not challenge these selectivity data for Kcnn4 KO.

Both address Kcnn4 KO effects on NLRP3 oligomerization and NEK7 binding (C151-C154). OpenEval finds support linking KCa3.1 to inflammasome assembly. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these mechanistic data.

Both evaluate in vivo Kcnn4 KO metabolic phenotype (C155-C158). OpenEval finds comprehensive support validating in vitro findings. Peer reviewers do not critique these in vivo Kcnn4 data, unlike their concerns about Trpm2 KO requiring cell-type-specific deletion.

Both address biphasic JNK activation with distinct temporal patterns (C159-C162). OpenEval finds support from time-course immunoblotting. Peer reviewers do not directly critique these JNK activation data.

Both evaluate temporal progression of Ca2+, K+, and ER Ca2+ changes (C163-C167). OpenEval finds time-course measurements supportive. Peer reviewers do not directly challenge these temporal data, though underlying Ca2+ measurement concerns may apply.

Both address JNK activation being necessary but insufficient for ASC phosphorylation (C168-C170). OpenEval finds temporal dissociation demonstrates this. Peer reviewers do not critique these ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization timing data.

Both evaluate Kcnn4 KO and Trpm2 KO effects on JNK phosphorylation (C171-C173). OpenEval finds support linking the Ca2+-K+ axis to JNK. Peer reviewers do not directly challenge these signaling connections.

Both address JNK inhibitor effects on ASC phosphorylation/oligomerization and IL-1β (C174-C177). OpenEval finds comprehensive support for JNK's role. Peer reviewers do not critique these pharmacological validation data.
Both evaluate ASK1-JNK pathway specificity using selonsertib (C178-C183). OpenEval finds strong support for pathway specificity. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these ASK1 inhibitor data.
Both address selonsertib effects on ASC oligomerization/phosphorylation (C184-C185). OpenEval finds support establishing ASK1 upstream of JNK. Peer reviewers do not challenge these data.

Both evaluate CaMKII mediating ASK1 phosphorylation using KN-93 vs KN-92 (C186-C188). OpenEval finds the inactive analog control strengthens conclusions. Peer reviewers do not critique these CaMKII data.
Both address CaMKII inhibitor effects on JNK and IL-1β (C189-C191). OpenEval finds support completing the mechanistic pathway. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these data.

Both evaluate the overarching integrated model (C192). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from all preceding results forming a coherent pathway. Peer reviewers conclude the model is only 'incompletely supported' because foundational lysosomal Ca2+ measurements, TRPM2 localization/function, ER→lysosome refilling, and SOCE activation are all challenged, despite KCa3.1 and CaMKII-ASK1-JNK components being supported.
